An 80% reimbursement is not an unlimited benefit: chart the annual cap and the cash needed first

Follow two benefit years, separate insurer payments from household costs and see why a service-year allowance and a reimbursement receipt belong in different calendars.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore two benefit years and the reimbursement cash calendar

Interactive planning lab

Reimbursements received after the twenty-fourth service month$0

Hypothetical single benefit category with confirmed eligible bills for 24 consecutive months, beginning at the start of a benefit year. Each twelve-month service year resets the deductible and insurer-payment maximum. The annual maximum caps benefit dollars, not eligible expenses. Deductible applies first, then the coverage percentage, then the remaining benefit maximum. Eligibility and prices are assumed confirmed independently; no claim adjudication is calculated. Each bill is paid before that month’s income allocation and reimbursement receipts arrive at month-end. Reimbursement follows the entered whole-month lag, including zero. A payment received in a later year still consumes the benefit year of its service. The chart continues after month 24 only to collect delayed receipts; no more bills or allocations occur then. No premiums, clinical decision, treatment scheduling advice, coordination of benefits, tax credit, policy interpretation, return or borrowing is modeled. Negative cash is an unfunded bill, not credit approval.

The central idea

A reimbursement percentage, deductible, annual insurer-payment maximum and receipt date each answer a different question. Apply them separately before deciding how much of an eligible bill the household must fund.

01

Read the percentage beside the deductible and annual maximum

A benefit description can display an attractive reimbursement percentage without saying how many dollars will be paid over a year. The percentage applies to an eligible amount under the relevant terms. A deductible can reduce that amount first, and an annual maximum can stop further insurer payments even when eligible bills continue.

The hypothetical example has CAD 400 of confirmed eligible expenses in each of twenty-four service months. Each twelve-month benefit year begins with a CAD 200 deductible and a CAD 1,500 maximum on insurer benefit dollars. The reimbursement share after the deductible is 80%.

The FCAC health-insurance overview identifies percentage coverage and annual maximum amounts as policy details to check. The calculator uses independently selected teaching terms. It does not determine whether a service, provider or charge is eligible under a real plan.

02

Apply the limits in a stated order

The model first applies the remaining annual deductible to the month’s eligible bill. It then multiplies the remainder by the reimbursement percentage. Finally, it caps the result at the unused insurer-payment maximum for that service year. A maximum on reimbursed dollars is different from a maximum on eligible expenses.

In month one, CAD 200 of the CAD 400 bill uses the deductible. Eighty percent of the remaining CAD 200 produces a CAD 160 allowed benefit. The following full eligible bill produces CAD 320, because the deductible has already been used.

Cumulative allowed benefits reach CAD 1,440 after month five. Month six has only CAD 60 of the annual maximum left, so its allowed benefit is CAD 60. Later bills in that service year receive zero in this example. The 80% percentage remains an input, but the remaining annual maximum has become the binding constraint.

03

Reconcile the household share without counting costs twice

Each service year contains CAD 4,800 of eligible expenses. The insurer allowance reaches CAD 1,500, leaving CAD 3,300 with the household. Across two service years, eligible expenses total CAD 9,600, allowed benefits total CAD 3,000 and the household portion is CAD 6,600.

The household share already includes the effect of the deductible, percentage cost sharing and expenses after the cap is exhausted. Adding the annual deductible to that CAD 3,300 again would double count part of the cost. The annual stacked bars keep the two complementary parts aligned with the full eligible expense total.

Premiums and ineligible charges are excluded. They would be additional household costs where applicable. The model also excludes other insurers, public reimbursement, negotiated provider adjustments and tax credits. Those items require their own confirmed terms and should not be inferred from the selected coverage percentage.

04

Separate the service year from the cash-receipt month

The default reimbursement arrives two whole months after the service bill, at month-end. A benefit allowed for service month one therefore arrives at the end of month three. The original bill is paid before that receipt. A claim allowance can be a receivable without being cash that can already pay another bill.

In this illustration, the maximum is charged to the year of service. A receipt in a later year does not create new room in the earlier service year or consume the following year’s cap. Month thirteen begins a new deductible and maximum because it starts the second modeled benefit year.

The cash chart continues beyond service month twenty-four when delayed receipts require a tail. No extra bills or income allocations are created in that tail. The headline separately reports benefits received after the final service month, which can be positive when the selected maximum allows benefits late in the second year.

05

Test the lowest cash point before resources arrive

The default assigns CAD 2,000 of starting cash and CAD 250 from income at each service month-end. Every bill is paid before that month-end allocation and any reimbursement. This ordering lets the model test the cash required before a covered expense is eventually reimbursed.

Under the defaults, the required starting cash is CAD 1,000. The selected CAD 2,000 reserve therefore covers the modeled calendar, and cash ends at CAD 1,400 after all receipts. The result reconciles as starting cash plus CAD 6,000 of allocations, less CAD 9,600 of bills, plus CAD 3,000 of reimbursements.

Changing the receipt lag does not alter the annual insurer/household cost split. It can alter the amount needed in advance. Even zero lag in this example means reimbursement at month-end after the bill, rather than money available before the bill or a direct-billing arrangement.

06

Review benefit mechanics and cash funding together

The matrix changes the reimbursement lag and annual insurer-payment maximum, then calculates extra starting cash after the selected reserve. It retains eligible bills, deductible, reimbursement percentage and the monthly allocation. Its cells describe financial stresses, without a probability of claim approval or an assessment of treatment needs.

Before relying on a real budget, confirm the benefit year, what the maximum measures, which deductible applies, the recognized eligible amount and the actual receipt process. Check whether several services share one maximum or whether separate limits apply. Reconcile benefits already used before treating the entire annual amount as available.

This article does not recommend changing treatment dates or make a clinical decision. The scheduled bills are externally confirmed assumptions. Its planning task is to keep cost sharing, annual benefit capacity and the money required before reimbursement visible together, then update the ledger when an insurer confirms the actual claim outcome.
